costGuide.title: Mercedes-Benz OM648 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an OM648 engine typically takes 10-14 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the swirl flap system, injector seals, and EGR cooler. failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM648 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Swirl Flap Motor Failure - All variants
items.whatHappens: The plastic gears inside the electronic swirl flap actuator motor strip over time, causing the ECU to throw a check engine light and default the engine to limp mode. In some cases, the flaps themselves can seize in the inlet manifold due to heavy EGR soot buildup.
items.repairVsReplace: The actuator motor can be replaced independently and relatively cheaply. However, if the flaps are seized or the manifold is heavily carboned, a full inlet manifold replacement or verified delete is required.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death") - All variants
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade, allowing high-pressure combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads, leading to a distinct tapping noise, rough idling, and a strong smell of exhaust in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: EGR Cooler Leaks - High-mileage units
items.whatHappens: The internal matrix of the EGR cooler can crack over time, leading to coolant loss, white smoke from the exhaust, or coolant entering the intake manifold.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR cooler replacement is a standard repair. If neglected, it can lead to overheating and place undue stress on the head gasket, though the OM648 block itself is highly resistant to catastrophic failure.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM648 is generally considered a highly robust inline-6, largely avoiding the catastrophic bottom-end bearing issues of later V6 designs. Units maintained with strict oil change intervals routinely exceed 250,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Mercedes-Benz OM648
variants.intro: The engine code is stamped on the left-hand side of the cylinder block, near the bellhousing. It will also be listed on your V5C logbook under "Engine Capacity" or visible via a VIN decode. The OM648 is sometimes confused with the older 3.0L inline-6 OM606 (which used pre-chamber indirect injection) or the later 3.0L V6 OM642. Fitting the wrong revision or assuming interchangeability matters significantly: the OM648 requires specific ECU mapping, common-rail injection plumbing, and engine mount configurations that will not function correctly if swapped with an OM606 or an OM642 without significant modification.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM648 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM648 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented replacement of the swirl flap actuator and injector seals. Given the age of these vehicles, the primary risk is hidden carbon buildup or degraded rubber components, so a compression test is mandatory before purchase.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM648 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will address the common failure points by upgrading or replacing the swirl flap system, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR cooler, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM648 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage W220 S-Class or W163 M-Class restorations where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM648 engine is installed by specialists familiar with early Mercedes CDI systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM648 is typically found in W211, W220, and W163 vehicles valued between £3,000 and £12,000, a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the host's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: How much does a Mercedes OM648 engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes OM648 engine typically costs between £2,800 and £4,500 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £3,450 to £5,400 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £1,200 but carry higher risk due to the engine's age. items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM648 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are swirl flap motor failure, injector seal weeping ("Black Death"), and EGR cooler leaks. Swirl flap motor failure triggers limp mode and is a routine fix, whereas injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup and rough idling but is a cheap and preventative maintenance item. Get quotes for a rebuilt OM648 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the OM648 engine?
items.answer: The OM648 was fitted to the W211 E-Class (E 320 CDI), the W220 S-Class (S 320 CDI), and the W163 M-Class (ML 320 CDI), serving as the definitive inline-6 diesel for these premium chassis between 2000 and 2005. Check your registration to confirm your exact OM648 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned OM648 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned OM648 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by upgrading or replacing the swirl flap system, fitting new injector seals, and refreshing the EGR cooler, whereas used engines often hide stretched components and carboned manifolds. items.answer: The OM648 is a distinct 3.2L inline-6 common-rail diesel, producing a unique sound and performance profile compared to the older pre-chamber OM606 or the later V6 OM642.
